options.text: Several separately deployed services that all read and write one shared database for simplicity
One deployable unit whose modules own their code and data and talk only through defined interfaces
A monolith kept small enough to run on a single server, with no horizontal scaling at all
A set of microservices packed into one container and deployed together as a single unit

explanation: A modular monolith keeps one deployable but enforces internal boundaries. (a) is a shared-database service setup, which couples services through their schemas. (c) is about how many servers run it; a monolith, modular or not, can run on many servers. (d) is a distributed system squeezed into one container, not a single codebase with enforced module boundaries.

prompt: Which of these are genuine benefits of microservices? Select all that apply.

options.text: Teams can deploy their service without coordinating a joint release
Calls between components become faster, since each service is small and focused
A CPU-heavy component can scale separately from the rest
Transactions that span components get simpler, since each service owns less data

explanation: Independent deploys and independent scaling are real benefits. (b) is backwards: network calls are much slower than in-process calls, however small the service. (d) is also backwards: you lose single-database transactions and need patterns like sagas.

prompt: A page makes 15 **sequential** calls to other services, each taking about 4 ms including the network hop. Roughly how much time do the calls alone add?

options.text: About 4 ms
About 15 ms
About 60 ms
About 600 ms

explanation: Sequential calls add up: 15 × 4 ms = 60 ms. (a) would only hold if all calls ran in parallel. (b) assumes 1 ms per call. (d) is ten times too high.

options.text: The number of services in a system tends to double every two years as the company grows
Systems tend to mirror the communication structure of the organisation that builds them
Every service must own exactly one database, which no other service may read directly
Adding more engineers to a project that is already late only makes it finish later

explanation: Conway (1968) observed that designs copy the communication structure of the team that builds them. (a) is a made-up growth rule. (c) is a microservice guideline (database per service), not Conway's law. (d) is Brooks's law, from The Mythical Man-Month.

scenario: A startup of 7 engineers is building its first product. The domain is still changing every few weeks. They have no CI/CD pipeline yet and log to files on each server. The CTO proposes 12 microservices from day one so they 'won't need to rewrite later'.

options.text: Agree: starting with microservices avoids a painful, risky split later once the product has grown
Start as a modular monolith with enforced boundaries, build deploy and logging tooling, split when needed
Build one service per developer, so each of the 7 engineers fully owns and deploys their own code
Build a monolith with no module boundaries at all, since boundaries only slow early teams down

explanation: A small team with a moving domain and no platform tooling will pay all the microservice costs without the coordination benefit, and will likely draw boundaries in the wrong places. (a) ignores that moving a service boundary is far more expensive than moving a module boundary. (c) ties services to people, not business capabilities. (d) leads to a big ball of mud that is hard to split later.

scenario: The orders service calls the payments service to charge a card. The call times out after 2 seconds. The payments service may or may not have charged the card.
prompt: What is the safest way for the orders service to handle this?

options.text: Retry the charge immediately with a fresh request, since the first one most likely never arrived
Mark the order as failed and ask the user to try again, since the call never got a success reply
Retry with the same idempotency key so payments spots a repeat, then reconcile from the result
Wrap the order write and the card charge in one database transaction so both commit or neither

explanation: A timeout means 'unknown', not 'failed'. Retrying with an idempotency key lets the payments service return the original result instead of charging twice. (a) risks a double charge: the first request may well have succeeded. (b) may leave a charged customer with a failed order. (d) is not possible across separate service databases.

scenario: A company has 8 services. Each release, they must deploy users, then orders, then billing, in that order, because they all read and write the same PostgreSQL tables and a schema change breaks the others.
prompt: What is this architecture usually called, and what is the root problem?

options.text: A modular monolith; the problem is simply that it has grown too many modules for one team
A distributed monolith; a shared database couples the services so none can deploy independently
An event-driven architecture; the problem is that services touch tables instead of publishing events
Healthy microservices; ordered deploys are normal whenever services depend on each other

explanation: Services that must deploy together because they share a schema are a distributed monolith: network costs without independence. (a) is wrong because a modular monolith is one deployable, not 8. (c) misnames the pattern; events alone would not fix the shared tables. (d) is wrong: independent deploys are the main point of services.

prompt: Which split usually works **worst** for microservices?

options.text: Orders, payments and catalog as separate services, each owned by its own team
A frontend service, a business-logic service and a database-access service
A separate notification service that consumes order and shipping events
A separate search service, fed by change events published from the catalog

explanation: Splitting by technical layer means almost every feature changes all three services, so teams must coordinate every release. (a), (c) and (d) split by business capability, which lets one team change one service for most features.

prompt: Which of these become **necessary** once a request crosses many services? Select all that apply.

options.text: A request ID passed through every hop
Distributed tracing
Timeouts on every outbound call
A single shared database for all services

explanation: Request IDs and tracing let you follow one request across services, and timeouts stop one slow dependency from hanging every caller. (d) is the opposite of the goal: a shared database couples services together.

options.text: Rewriting the whole monolith from scratch in parallel and switching over in one big release
Moving one capability at a time from the old system to a new service until the old code can go
Throttling an overloaded service so it sheds requests gradually instead of failing all at once
Merging small, chatty microservices back into a single monolith one service at a time

explanation: The strangler fig grows around the old system and gradually replaces it, one route at a time. (a) is the big-bang rewrite the pattern exists to avoid. (c) describes load shedding or throttling. (d) is the opposite direction.
